diagnosis.what_is_wrong: A short-lived `ttworker` workload consumed essentially all four CPUs while it ran, plausibly extending the coding task by leaving little CPU capacity for other work. This is evidence of a brief CPU-saturation episode, not proof that scheduler wait alone explains the task’s full duration.
diagnosis.evidence: Compared the quiet pre-period (02:46:06.400–02:46:11.000) with active execution (02:46:11.100–02:46:14.900) using the workers’ whole-trace `sched_stat_runtime` aggregation: total CPU use rose from 1.725 CPU-seconds over 4.6 seconds (0.375 CPU-s/wall-s) to 15.062 CPU-seconds over 3.8 seconds (3.964 CPU-s/wall-s), with `ttworker` accounting for 14.837 CPU-seconds (98.5%). `ctf_proclife` places this process in the same container from 02:46:11.000 to 02:46:14.800; raw scheduler lines show its threads switching among themselves on CPUs 0–3 with `prev_state=0`, and runtime samples near 1 ms per 100 ms per core. Checked competing explanations: block request counts fell rather than rose, dirty pages were far below thresholds, network samples showed successful transmissions, and `ttworker` had no futex entries. Wakeup-to-switch delay was not quantitatively correlated, so CPU starvation delay specifically is not established.
diagnosis.window_evidence: `ttworker` first appears at 02:46:11.000; its measured runtime is already high in the 02:46:11.100–11.200 bucket, then stays near four CPU-seconds per wall-second through the 02:46:14.800 bucket. Its last-seen time is 02:46:14.800 and active-window runtime measurement ends at 02:46:14.900, after which the total CPU rate drops sharply.
